title: Sojourner Truth: She Could Not Read, but Her Voice Woke a Nation | 143 Years Ago Today

lines: She never learned to read or write, yet her voice woke a nation.

On this day in eighteen eighty-three,

data.name: Sojourner Truth

lines: Born into slavery in New York around 1797,
Born into slavery in New York around seventeen ninety-seven,
she was named Isabella, and grew up speaking Dutch.
At nine, she was sold along with a flock of sheep.
In 1826, her owner broke his word. She left with her baby.
In eighteen twenty-six, when her owner broke his promise, she walked to freedom with her baby.
Her son Peter was illegally sold to the South.
So a mother who could not read took a white man to court.
In 1828, she won and brought her son home.
In eighteen twenty-eight, she won and brought her son home.
She was among the first Black women to win such a case.
She was among the first Black women in America to win such a case.
In 1843, she gave herself a new name: Sojourner Truth.
In eighteen forty-three, she gave herself a new name: Sojourner Truth.
She would travel, and speak the truth.
In 1851, she rose to speak at a women's rights convention,
In eighteen fifty-one, she rose to speak at a women's rights convention,
remembered today by the words: Ain't I a woman?
She sold small photo cards of herself to fund her work.
They read: I sell the shadow to support the substance.
In 1864, she met President Lincoln at the White House.
In eighteen sixty-four, she met President Lincoln at the White House.
After the war, she helped freed people find work and land.
She died on November 26, 1883, in Michigan.
She died on November twenty-sixth, eighteen eighty-three, in Michigan.
She never learned to read,
yet the world still remembers her voice.
Her question for you:
If the world won't let you speak, how will you be heard?
